**Lab pack:** [lab03.tar.gz](../labs/lab03.tar.gz) — pre-placed on lab machines, downloadable for home practice.

**Evaluation:** **graded** — equal share of the 20% lab component. Three graded problems, five fill-in-the-blank programs, and sixteen drills, plus observed work and a short viva. Teams of 1–2; pairs swap driver/navigator at half-time.

::: {.callout-note}
**Nothing new today.** No new constructs, no new syntax. Everything here is Week 3 —
types, variables, assignment, operators and precedence — met again, from a different
angle, until it is automatic. Lab 02 asked you to *write* programs. Today mostly asks
you to *predict* them, which is harder and more useful.
:::

## The two things that went wrong last time

We fixed both in the pack, so read this once:

**1. People got lost.** So this week the installer does not tell you where to go — it
**puts you there**, and changes your prompt to prove it:

```
[lab03 OK w04-l03-ee-sd]$
```

If you can see `[lab03 OK ...]` at the left of your cursor, you are in the right place.
If you cannot, you are not. There is now exactly one command to remember, and it works
from anywhere at all:

```bash
./where.sh
```

It never changes anything. It tells you where you are, where your workspace is, and
prints the exact line to copy to get back.

**2. People lost marks on formatting, not on thinking.** So this week **the final
`printf` is already written for you** in every file. You cannot get the output format
wrong, because you are not writing it. If the checker says `WRONG`, it means your
*computation* is wrong — which is a much more useful thing to be told.

## Act 0 · Land (10 min)

Pack pre-placed on machines, or:

```bash
wget https://acads-iit-jammu.github.io/csp-f26-dhavala/labs/lab03.tar.gz
```

```bash
tar xzf lab03.tar.gz
cd lab03
./install.sh
```

It will drop you inside your workspace with the new prompt. Then start the recorder:

```bash
script session.txt
```

The transcript travels in your bundle and is the proof of your own work.

::: {.callout-important}
Do not go any further until your prompt shows `[lab03 OK ...]`. If it does not, run
`./where.sh` and paste the line it gives you.
:::

## Act 1 · Drills — predict, then run (35 min)

Sixteen tiny programs. For each one you will **see the code, write down what you think
it prints, and only then run it**.

```bash
./drill.sh --all
```

Predicting is the exercise. Running is only the marking. A wrong prediction is worth
exactly as many marks as a right one — but only if you actually write it down first, so
be honest with yourself. The one thing that earns nothing is running the program before
you have committed to an answer.

What they cover:

| Drills | Territory |
|---|---|
| d01–d04 | integer vs. real division, `%` with negatives, where a cast goes |
| d05–d08 | precedence, associativity, `*=`, chained assignment |
| d09–d12 | characters as numbers, truncation, deriving the case gap |
| d13–d14 | what `printf` rounds, pads, and refuses to add |
| s1–s2 | *(stretch)* a comparison is a value; why `%` refuses floats |

`./drill.sh` on its own shows your progress. `./drill.sh 7` re-runs just number 7.

::: {.callout-tip}
Drill 04 is the single most expensive misconception in this course. If you get it wrong,
stop and stare at it until it is obvious — it comes back in `f2`, `f5` and `e2`.
:::

## Act 2 · Fill in the blanks (35 min)

Five complete programs. The declarations are written, the `scanf` is written, the final
`printf` is written. **Only the expressions are missing**, marked `/* TODO */`.

| File | Program | Blanks |
|---|---|---|
| `f1_money.c` | paise → rupees and paise | 2 |
| `f2_average.c` | average of three integers, 2 decimals | 1 |
| `f3_swap.c` | swap two variables | 3 — *and the order matters* |
| `f4_upper.c` | a lowercase letter → uppercase + its code | 2 |
| `f5_temp.c` | Celsius → Fahrenheit | 1 |

Check them one at a time as you go:

```bash
./check.sh f1
```

The shipped files **do not compile** until you fill the blanks — that is expected, and
the compiler will point straight at the `/* TODO */` you have not done yet.

## Act 3 · The graded three (30 min, solo)

Same shape: everything written except the computation.

| Problem | Task | Final line ends with exactly |
|---|---|---|
| `e1.c` | total inches → feet and inches | `feet=<F> inches=<I>` |
| `e2.c` | percentage scored, 2 decimals | `pct=<P>` |
| `e3.c` | an uppercase letter → lowercase + its code | `lower=<C> code=<N>` |

Each one is a relative of something you have already done today: `e1` is `f1` with a
different divisor, `e2` is the `f2` trap in new clothes, and `e3` is `f4` held up to a
mirror — same gap, opposite direction. Work out the direction rather than guessing it.

**How checking works** — as in Lab 02: `./check.sh e1` compiles *your source* and runs
it on the public inputs from the spec **and on fresh random inputs drawn from the
GIVEN**. A program that memorises the example fails the next draw. Only one that
computes survives.

## Act 4 · Check, fix, bundle (10 min)

```bash
./check.sh
```

Fix, re-check, repeat. Then — green or time-up (an imperfect bundle beats no bundle):

```bash
./check.sh --bundle
```

Carry `../lab03_<rolls>_<branch>_w<NN>.tar.gz` out with you (Moodle + email yourself).
The machine forgets.

## Stretch (fast finishers)

- Do drills `s1` and `s2` if you skipped them.
- **Round, don't truncate.** `e1` throws away the leftover inches. Using only `/`, `%`
  and `+`, print the number of feet *rounded to the nearest foot* instead. No `if`, no
  library. (Hint: what happens if you add half a foot before dividing?)
- **Break `f2`.** Find three inputs in the GIVEN where an average computed with `/3`
  and one computed with `/3.0` differ by as much as possible. Put them in
  `notes/answers.txt`.

## Reflect

✍️ Into `notes/answers.txt`: look back at your `notes/drills.log`. Pick the one drill you
got most wrong. In two sentences — what did you believe before you ran it, and what do
you believe now?
